findings.issue_text: [BUG] The new authenticated-user-vs-sender verification only runs in the branch where the Integration already exists; in the fresh-install branch (Integration.DoesNotExist) the pipeline advances to the next step with no comparison between pipeline.state['github_authenticated_user'] and the installation's webhook sender, so the acceptance criterion 'the GitHub user who authorizes must be the user who installed the app' is silently dropped for first-time installs. A user who completes the new OAuth step as themselves can bind an installation_id belonging to a different GitHub account's brand-new installation (installation ids are enumerable) via the installation_id GET parameter and complete setup; the security property this change introduces is enforced only on the reinstall path, leaving the primary install path unguarded.

[ADVISORY] The mandatory OAuthLoginView is inserted into get_pipeline_views with no feature flag or rollout gate, and pipelines created before the deploy lack the github_authenticated_user state that the new GitHubInstallation check requires. Any user mid-installation at the time of deploy who returns to the pipeline after it ships hits the sender check with fetch_state('github_authenticated_user') returning None, gets the generic 'Invalid installation request.' page, and must restart the whole install flow; an operator cannot disable the new step without a code rollback.

[ADVISORY] The authorize URL is assembled by raw string concatenation without urlencode() for state or redirect_uri, unlike the urlencoded flows used elsewhere in the codebase. If absolute_uri(reverse('sentry-extension-setup', ...)) ever produces a redirect_uri containing reserved query characters (e.g. a query string added to the setup route), the constructed authorize URL silently mangles the parameters; the next change to this URL shape is riskier because encoding is not handled here.

[BUG] The sender-vs-authenticated-user check reads integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] and crashes with KeyError (returning a 500) for any pre-existing GitHub Integration whose metadata lacks a 'sender' key. Any operator running the install-completion flow against an integration row created before sender was recorded (or created via API/migration without sender) gets an unhandled exception instead of the intended error page or a pass-through, breaking the install flow entirely for legacy data.

[ADVISORY] Under-scoping: the 'authenticated GitHub user must match the installation sender' invariant is enforced only in the branch where an Integration already exists and is unlinked; the Integration.DoesNotExist branch (fresh install) calls pipeline.next_step() with no sender verification. The stated security goal (bind an installation to the GitHub account that actually authorized) is not enforced on the fresh-install path; a crafted installation_id for an installation whose integration row has not yet been created (webhook delayed/lost) completes the install with no sender check, so the guarantee is only partial. Author rebuttal is that GitHub only redirects the installing user back — but the code accepts arbitrary installation_id query params, so the invariant is bypassable precisely where it matters most.

[ADVISORY] OAuthLoginView duplicates token-exchange logic that already exists in OAuth2CallbackView/identity providers (manual safe_urlopen + parse_qsl instead of reusing the existing exchange helper), creating a second hand-maintained copy of the OAuth callback protocol. The next change to the OAuth exchange (error handling, param encoding, GHES variants) must be made in two places; the inline copy also swallows all exceptions with a bare except that returns the generic error, masking real config errors (bad client secret) as 'invalid installation request' with no logging.

[ADVISORY] The authorize redirect interpolates redirect_uri into the query string without URL-encoding, and client_id/state likewise, so any future parameter containing reserved characters silently corrupts the query. Works today only because the URI happens to contain no & or =; the next edit to redirect_uri or addition of a parameter breaks the authorize request against GitHub, and the failure shows up as a GitHub-side OAuth error rather than a code-level error.

[ADVISORY] installation_id is bound into pipeline state directly from request.GET with no validation, and is now bound in two places (OAuthLoginView and GitHubInstallation) with the later value silently overwriting the earlier. A tampered installation_id query parameter on the callback leg overwrites the one captured at the authorize step, defeating the point of carrying it through signed pipeline state; the duplicated bind_state also means the next maintainer must reason about two write sites for one state key.

[ADVISORY] Coverage gap: the new OAuth failure branches in OAuthLoginView — invalid state, token exchange failure (no access_token in response), and get_user_info missing 'login' — have no test in this diff; all tests stub a successful exchange. A regression in any of the three error returns (e.g., the state comparison or the payload parsing) would ship undetected, and the attacker-relevant invalid-state path is exactly the branch a future refactor is most likely to break.

[ADVISORY] Refactor churn not traceable to the security requirement: the FORWARD_INSTALL_FOR constant and its comment were deleted and re-inlined as provider_id == "github" with an identical comment, a no-op behavioral edit inside a security PR. Diff noise that obscures the actual security change during review/audit; the removal of the list constant also forecloses the extension point if a second provider ever needs the same forwarding, for zero benefit in this change.

[ADVISORY] The dispatch performs two separate Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) lookups (the first without a status filter inside the try block, the second with status=ACTIVE), duplicating the query and splitting the status logic across two branches. Every setup request does redundant DB work and the next editor must reason about two divergent fetch conditions (one status-agnostic, one ACTIVE-only); a single status-filtered lookup with a DoesNotExist->error branch makes the double-query and the split condition unnecessary.

[ADVISORY] The authorize redirect builds the query string by f-string interpolation without URL-encoding redirect_uri (which contains '://' and '/'), producing a technically malformed query component. The behavior currently works because GitHub tolerates it, but any future change that adds query parameters after redirect_uri, or a stricter client/proxy, will mis-parse the unencoded value; urlencode() on the params dict removes the fragility at zero cost.

[ADVISORY] OAuthLoginView binds installation_id straight from request.GET into pipeline state with no format or ownership validation, and GitHubInstallation later re-reads it from GET with priority over the bound state, so the pipeline value is overwritten by raw query input at both stages. The pipeline state copy of installation_id is not a trusted snapshot: anyone crafting the final callback URL supplies the installation_id that all downstream checks (OrganizationIntegration existence, sender match) evaluate, so any future check added on the bound state can be bypassed by supplying a different GET value.

[ADVISORY] Adding OAuthLoginView unconditionally as the first pipeline view changes the direct-from-GitHub post-install redirect path (setup_action=install forwarded by pipeline_advancer) to require a full OAuth authorize round-trip before reaching GitHubInstallation. Existing users whose browsers land on the setup URL with installation_id and no code/state are silently redirected to GitHub's authorize screen instead of the app-install page; for users not currently logged into GitHub this introduces an extra auth prompt in a flow that previously went straight to installation handling — a behavioral contract change for the direct-install entry point with no opt-out.

[ADVISORY] The token-exchange failure path (non-200 response, unparseable body, missing access_token) and the user-info failure path both collapse into the generic 'Invalid installation request' error, discarding the GitHub error payload (e.g. bad_verification_code, expired code) that distinguishes a transient OAuth failure from a tampering attempt. Support and users cannot distinguish 'restart the flow' (expired code, transient GitHub error) from a genuine validation failure; the error() helper's separate error_short/error_long parameters exist but this branch never uses them, so the next fix must re-derive which failure occurred.

[ADVISORY] The FORWARD_INSTALL_FOR list was replaced by an inline provider_id == "github" literal in the condition, hardcoding the provider key in the generic pipeline advancer that is shared by IntegrationPipeline and IdentityProviderPipeline. The next provider needing the same direct-install forwarding must edit generic shared code (or copy the pattern into another conditional), and the 'github' magic string is now duplicated between pipeline_advancer.py and the GitHub integration module with nothing tying them together; a provider-key constant or per-provider hook removes the cross-module literal.

[BUG] The installer-identity check is only enforced on the re-install branch; the first-time-install branch (Integration.DoesNotExist -> pipeline.next_step()) skips the github_authenticated_user vs integration.metadata['sender']['login'] comparison entirely, so the stated security objective of the review iteration is not preserved on the primary path it was added for. An attacker who causes a victim to install the GitHub App (victim is the sender per the webhook) and then completes the Sentry-side flow under their own OAuth identity gets a first-time integration created with no sender match — the exact scenario the accepted fix claims to close — while only the pre-existing-integration path is protected.

[ADVISORY] The new hard requirement that the Sentry-side OAuth user equal the original GitHub 'sender' login silently changes the accepted install contract: previously any authenticated org member completing the flow with a valid installation_id could finish setup; review iterations introduced this constraint without a separately accepted change of objective. Legitimate operators get locked out: e.g. an admin who uninstalls/reinstalls after the original 'sender' has left the org or changed their GitHub login can never complete installation — GitHubInstallation returns the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error page with no remediation path, and there is no option/flag to disable the new behavior without a code deploy.

[ADVISORY] Review iterations collapsed three distinct user-facing error messages (invalid request, pending deletion, installed on another org) through one generic default while also replacing the distinct 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' message with the new generic ERR_INTEGRATION_INVALID_INSTALLATION_REQUEST — a user-facing copy change smuggled in by the refactor rather than explicitly accepted. Users hitting the not-found case now see 'Invalid installation request / restart the installation process' instead of the previous accurate message, and support docs/ticket triage keyed to the old strings no longer match; the support-staff-visible contract drifted silently.

[ADVISORY] The OAuth authorize redirect is assembled by raw string interpolation (client_id, state, redirect_uri unencoded) instead of urlencode, diverging from how every other OAuth client in the codebase builds this URL. If any of these values ever contain reserved query characters (e.g. a client_id or redirect base with '&' or '='), the authorize URL is silently corrupted and the flow breaks at GitHub with no parseable error; the next person extending this URL inherits a hand-built query string.

[ADVISORY] The token-exchange block re-implements OAuth2CallbackView.exchange_token/get_token_params by hand (comment even says 'similar to'), creating a parallel hand-maintained copy of standard OAuth exchange logic including its own swallow-all exception handler that discards the GitHub error response. Any failure mode the shared implementation already handles (error=access_denied callback, non-form-encoded token responses, non-200 exchange responses) gets flattened into the generic 'Invalid installation request.' page with the root cause discarded (the except clause drops req status/body), making the new flow undebuggable for the next change; extracting/reusing the existing view logic would delete this entire duplicate branch set.

[BUG] The new authenticated-sender check is only applied on the branch where the Integration already exists; in the Integration.DoesNotExist branch the pipeline proceeds to the next step with an attacker-supplied installation_id and no verification that the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user owns that installation. A user who completes the GitHub OAuth step as themselves can supply any installation_id that has no existing Sentry Integration row and link that installation (and its repository access) to their own organization, without being the person who installed the GitHub app. The diff adds the sender-vs-authenticated-user check precisely to prevent this, but only guards the already-linked path, leaving the first-install path — the more impactful case — open to the same cross-account claim.

[BUG] integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] raises KeyError for any existing integration whose metadata lacks a 'sender' key, crashing the install flow with a 500 instead of the intended error page. Integrations created before this change (or by code paths that do not store a 'sender' in metadata) hit an unhandled KeyError in GitHubInstallation.dispatch; the user sees a server error rather than the success/failure dialog, and the postMessage contract with the opener window is never satisfied, leaving the installer popup hung.

[ADVISORY] installation_id is bound to pipeline state in two independent places (OAuthLoginView from request.GET, GitHubInstallation from GET-or-state), creating parallel write paths for the same pipeline key with different validation timing. The next maintainer adding validation or normalization to one bind site (e.g. scoping or type-checking the installation_id) will not know the other path bypasses it; the GitHubInstallation view already silently prefers request.GET over the previously-bound state, so a request-supplied installation_id can overwrite the OAuth-step-bound value mid-pipeline.

[BUG] test_installation_not_found overwrites the first response with a second client.get and replaces the specific assertion ("The GitHub installation could not be found.") with a generic one ("Invalid installation request."), so the test no longer verifies the not-found behavior it is named for. If the not-found handling regresses (e.g. the new code's DoesNotExist branch inside the try in GitHubInstallation.dispatch returns next_step instead of error), this test still passes as long as any error page is rendered; the specific user-facing 'installation could not be found' message is now completely unasserted, and the first GET's response is silently discarded.

[BUG] test_github_user_mismatch asserts only the generic default error text 'Invalid installation request.', which is the response produced by every failure branch in OAuthLoginView and GitHubInstallation.dispatch (state mismatch, missing access_token, missing login, inactive integration, sender mismatch), so it cannot distinguish the sender-mismatch branch it claims to test from any other failure. Deleting or breaking the new `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` check does not necessarily fail this test: if the mismatch path were silently bypassed (e.g. metadata missing 'sender' raising, or the check inverted in a way that still errors elsewhere), the test passes as long as some failure page renders. The security-critical sender-verification branch has no assertion that specifically confirms the mismatch was the rejection reason.

[ADVISORY] The state value '9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3' is hardcoded and reused verbatim across four different tests and two different organizations, coupling the tests to the exact hash output of pipeline.signature. Any change to how Pipeline.signature is derived (salt, session key, provider key) breaks five assertions simultaneously and forces a blind find-and-replace of a magic constant; a copy-paste error during such a change would make tests assert against a wrong-but-consistent state value and pass while the real state-check logic diverges from what is exercised.

[ADVISORY] `auth_header = responses.calls[2].request.headers["Authorization"]` is index-coupled to the new OAuth exchange calls registered in _stub_github, asserting on a positional mock-call index rather than on behavior. Adding or reordering any mocked HTTP call in _stub_github (e.g. an extra /user call) silently shifts the index and makes this assertion validate a different request's header — the test keeps passing while verifying the wrong call, or fails confusingly with no behavioral change.

[ADVISORY] _stub_github now unconditionally registers the OAuth access_token and /user mocks for every test in the class, including tests that do not intend to exercise the OAuth exchange, and no test exercises the failure branches of the exchange (`except Exception: payload = {}` and 'access_token' not in payload). The swallowed-exception path and the missing-access_token path in OAuthLoginView (integration.py lines ~434-437) have zero coverage: a regression that makes safe_urlread failure crash with a 500 instead of rendering the error page would pass CI, because the only mocks registered always return a valid token body.

[ADVISORY] In test_github_installed_on_another_org and test_github_prevent_install_until_pending_deletion_is_complete, the initial `resp = self.client.get(self.init_path)` result is immediately overwritten by the follow-up setup_path GET, so no assertion ever inspects the first response. The init step's contract (e.g. that it redirects into the pipeline rather than erroring, and that it does not itself render the failure page) is unverified; if init started rendering the failure page directly the tests would still pass, masking a broken redirect flow behind the overwritten variable.

[ADVISORY] The state-mismatch rejection branch (`request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`) in OAuthLoginView is reached by no test in the diff; every setup-path test supplies the exact matching signature. A regression that weakens the state comparison (e.g. comparing only a prefix, or accepting any state) would not be caught by any test in this diff, despite this being the CSRF-defensive check the whole OAuth round-trip depends on. Checked test files: tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py — no test sends a mismatched or missing state value to the setup endpoint.

[BUG] get_user_info() in OAuthLoginView.dispatch is called outside the try/except that guards the token exchange, so any network/JSON failure fetching /user raises an unhandled exception and the user gets a raw 500 instead of the github-integration-failed error page the rest of the view guarantees. A transient GitHub API outage or malformed /user response during the install pipeline produces an unhandled exception (500 page) mid-pipeline; the pipeline state is left bound (github_authenticated_user never set) and the user sees a server error rather than the 'restart the installation' message every other failure path renders.

[BUG] integration.metadata['sender']['login'] raises KeyError for an ACTIVE Integration whose metadata lacks a 'sender' key, turning the install request into a 500 instead of the 4xx-style error page the contract of every other rejection path in this view provides. A pre-existing integration row created by an older flow (or by the webhook path before sender was recorded) that has no OrganizationIntegration yet crashes the pipeline with KeyError/500; the user cannot complete or even cleanly fail the install for that installation_id.

[ADVISORY] The sender-login equality check hard-requires pipeline state 'github_authenticated_user', so any pipeline session created before this deploy (or any entry path that skips OAuthLoginView) fails with None != login and the generic 'Invalid installation request' error during a rolling deploy. Users mid-installation when this code ships have no 'github_authenticated_user' in their session pipeline state; their previously-valid install now dead-ends on the generic error page with no way to distinguish skew from an actual attack, and no feature flag to revert without a code deploy.

[ADVISORY] Every failure path in OAuthLoginView (bad state, failed token exchange, missing access_token, missing login) collapses into the identical generic error page with no logging, metric, or distinction, so production failures of the new OAuth exchange are silent and indistinguishable from each other. Operators debugging install failures get zero signal — a GitHub-side token-exchange outage, a state mismatch caused by cache eviction of the pipeline, and an actual forged-state attempt all look identical with no log line or metric, making the 'restart the installation process' advice unverifiable and the failure rate unmeasurable.

[ADVISORY] The authorize redirect URL is built by f-string interpolation without urlencode, so state and redirect_uri (which contains '://', '/', and ':') are injected raw into the query string. The request works only because GitHub's parser tolerates unencoded reserved characters in redirect_uri; any change to the route (e.g. a query param on the setup URL) or stricter GitHub-side parsing silently breaks the OAuth leg, and the value cannot be safely extended without rework.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new `OAuthLoginView` that performs a manual OAuth token exchange (`safe_urlopen` to `get_oauth_access_token_url()`, then `safe_urlread(...).decode` + `dict(parse_qsl(body))`) with comments noting similarity to `OAuth2CallbackView.get_token_params`/`exchange_token`, rather than reusing a shared helper. It also wraps parsing in a broad `except Exception` and silently falls back to `{}` before returning the generic `error(...)`, with no logging, which can reduce debuggability (e.g., bad client secret/network issues presented as “Invalid installation request”). This is a concrete maintainability/observability concern grounded in the added code, not a directly provable functional defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The authorize redirect interpolates redirect_uri into the query string without URL-encoding, and client_id/state likewise, so any future parameter containing reserved characters silently corrupts the query. Works today only because the URI happens to contain no & or =; the next edit to redirect_uri or addition of a parameter breaks the authorize request against GitHub, and the failure shows up as a GitHub-side OAuth error rather than a code-level error.

adjudication.rationale: In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, the authorize URL is built via f-string: `...?client_id={github_client_id}&state={state}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}` without using `urlencode`/escaping. With the current `redirect_uri` (`absolute_uri(reverse(...))`) it contains no `&`/`=` so it works, but the construction is fragile: any future change where `redirect_uri` (or other params) contains query separators would corrupt the outbound GitHub authorize request. The diff shows the unencoded interpolation, but not an immediate broken behavior today.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] installation_id is bound into pipeline state directly from request.GET with no validation, and is now bound in two places (OAuthLoginView and GitHubInstallation) with the later value silently overwriting the earlier. A tampered installation_id query parameter on the callback leg overwrites the one captured at the authorize step, defeating the point of carrying it through signed pipeline state; the duplicated bind_state also means the next maintainer must reason about two write sites for one state key.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `installation_id` being written to the same pipeline state key in two places, and the later write can be sourced directly from `request.GET`. In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, `installation_id = request.GET.get("installation_id")` is immediately `pipeline.bind_state("installation_id", installation_id)` before redirecting to GitHub OAuth. Then in `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, `installation_id = request.GET.get("installation_id", pipeline.fetch_state("installation_id"))` prefers the query param over the signed state, and then calls `pipeline.bind_state("installation_id", installation_id)` again. This means a callback request that includes a tampered `installation_id` query parameter will override the earlier captured value, undermining the purpose of carrying it through pipeline state and creating two write sites maintainers must reason about.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Coverage gap: the new OAuth failure branches in OAuthLoginView — invalid state, token exchange failure (no access_token in response), and get_user_info missing 'login' — have no test in this diff; all tests stub a successful exchange. A regression in any of the three error returns (e.g., the state comparison or the payload parsing) would ship undetected, and the attacker-relevant invalid-state path is exactly the branch a future refactor is most likely to break.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds three early-error branches in `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`: invalid `state` (`if request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`), missing `access_token` in the parsed token response, and missing `login` from `get_user_info`. The new/updated tests stub a successful token exchange (`body=f"access_token={access_token}"`) and a successful `/user` response (`json={"login": "octocat"}`), so the `no access_token` and `no login` error returns are not exercised. However, the finding overstates the gap by also claiming the invalid-state branch is untested: `test_installation_not_found` now calls the setup endpoint with a mismatched `state` and asserts `b"Invalid installation request."`, which covers that branch.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Refactor churn not traceable to the security requirement: the FORWARD_INSTALL_FOR constant and its comment were deleted and re-inlined as provider_id == "github" with an identical comment, a no-op behavioral edit inside a security PR. Diff noise that obscures the actual security change during review/audit; the removal of the list constant also forecloses the extension point if a second provider ever needs the same forwarding, for zero benefit in this change.

adjudication.rationale: The diff in `pipeline_advancer.py` removes `FORWARD_INSTALL_FOR = ["github"]` (and its comment) and replaces the check `provider_id in FORWARD_INSTALL_FOR` with `provider_id == "github"`, while reintroducing the same comment inline. This is a no-op behavior change that adds churn/diff noise in a security-focused PR and also removes the small extension point of supporting multiple providers via the list constant, for no benefit shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The dispatch performs two separate Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) lookups (the first without a status filter inside the try block, the second with status=ACTIVE), duplicating the query and splitting the status logic across two branches. Every setup request does redundant DB work and the next editor must reason about two divergent fetch conditions (one status-agnostic, one ACTIVE-only); a single status-filtered lookup with a DoesNotExist->error branch makes the double-query and the split condition unnecessary.

adjudication.rationale: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, the diff shows two separate `Integration.objects.get` lookups by `external_id`: first inside the `try` used to compute `installations_exist` (`Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)`), and later another lookup with an additional status constraint (`Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)`). This is redundant DB work on every setup request and splits the “which integration statuses are acceptable” logic across two branches. It’s a maintainability/performance concern rather than a clear correctness defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The authorize redirect builds the query string by f-string interpolation without URL-encoding redirect_uri (which contains '://' and '/'), producing a technically malformed query component. The behavior currently works because GitHub tolerates it, but any future change that adds query parameters after redirect_uri, or a stricter client/proxy, will mis-parse the unencoded value; urlencode() on the params dict removes the fragility at zero cost.

adjudication.rationale: In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, the authorize URL is assembled via f-string (`...&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}`) rather than via `urlencode()`. The `redirect_uri` is built from `absolute_uri(reverse(...))` and contains `://` and `/`, and while this will usually work (and tests assert it), it is more fragile than encoding params (e.g., if `redirect_uri` ever gains its own `?`/`&` or other reserved chars). This is a robustness/maintainability concern rather than a verifiable current functional bug in the shown diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OAuthLoginView binds installation_id straight from request.GET into pipeline state with no format or ownership validation, and GitHubInstallation later re-reads it from GET with priority over the bound state, so the pipeline value is overwritten by raw query input at both stages. The pipeline state copy of installation_id is not a trusted snapshot: anyone crafting the final callback URL supplies the installation_id that all downstream checks (OrganizationIntegration existence, sender match) evaluate, so any future check added on the bound state can be bypassed by supplying a different GET value.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show `OAuthLoginView` storing `installation_id` directly from `request.GET` into pipeline state (`pipeline.bind_state("installation_id", installation_id)`), and `GitHubInstallation.dispatch` later computes `installation_id = request.GET.get("installation_id", pipeline.fetch_state("installation_id"))`, meaning any present query param overrides the previously bound state before being re-bound again. That makes the pipeline state copy of `installation_id` non-authoritative and potentially confusing as a “trusted snapshot.” However, the finding’s security-bypass framing is partly speculative (it talks about “any future check”); the current code consistently uses the (possibly GET-derived) `installation_id` for its checks, so this is more of a trust/flow/maintainability concern than a clearly demonstrated defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Adding OAuthLoginView unconditionally as the first pipeline view changes the direct-from-GitHub post-install redirect path (setup_action=install forwarded by pipeline_advancer) to require a full OAuth authorize round-trip before reaching GitHubInstallation. Existing users whose browsers land on the setup URL with installation_id and no code/state are silently redirected to GitHub's authorize screen instead of the app-install page; for users not currently logged into GitHub this introduces an extra auth prompt in a flow that previously went straight to installation handling — a behavioral contract change for the direct-install entry point with no opt-out.

adjudication.rationale: The diff unconditionally prepends `OAuthLoginView()` to the pipeline (`get_pipeline_views` now returns `[OAuthLoginView(), GitHubInstallation()]`). In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, when there is no `state` query param it immediately redirects to GitHub OAuth authorize (`/login/oauth/authorize`) regardless of whether `installation_id` is already present. Previously, the first view was `GitHubInstallation`, which would redirect to the GitHub App page (`https://github.com/apps/...`) when `installation_id` was missing, and otherwise proceed without an OAuth round-trip. Tests were updated to expect this new redirect sequence (first to OAuth authorize, then to `/apps/...`). This confirms a non-optional flow change for the setup entry point; it's a behavioral/UX contract change rather than a clear correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The token-exchange failure path (non-200 response, unparseable body, missing access_token) and the user-info failure path both collapse into the generic 'Invalid installation request' error, discarding the GitHub error payload (e.g. bad_verification_code, expired code) that distinguishes a transient OAuth failure from a tampering attempt. Support and users cannot distinguish 'restart the flow' (expired code, transient GitHub error) from a genuine validation failure; the error() helper's separate error_short/error_long parameters exist but this branch never uses them, so the next fix must re-derive which failure occurred.

adjudication.rationale: In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, multiple distinct failure modes all return the same `error(request, self.active_organization)` without inspecting/propagating GitHub’s error details: token exchange parsing errors and missing `access_token` (`payload = dict(parse_qsl(body))` then `if "access_token" not in payload: return error(...)`), and user info failures (`authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(...)` then `if "login" not in authenticated_user_info: return error(...)`). The code also does not check the token endpoint HTTP status or parse `error`/`error_description` fields. While this may be intentional for security/UX, the finding is correct that the new helper’s `error_short/error_long` isn’t leveraged here to distinguish OAuth transient issues vs validation/tampering, making support diagnosis harder.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The FORWARD_INSTALL_FOR list was replaced by an inline provider_id == "github" literal in the condition, hardcoding the provider key in the generic pipeline advancer that is shared by IntegrationPipeline and IdentityProviderPipeline. The next provider needing the same direct-install forwarding must edit generic shared code (or copy the pattern into another conditional), and the 'github' magic string is now duplicated between pipeline_advancer.py and the GitHub integration module with nothing tying them together; a provider-key constant or per-provider hook removes the cross-module literal.

adjudication.rationale: The diff removes `FORWARD_INSTALL_FOR = ["github"]` from `pipeline_advancer.py` and replaces the generic check `provider_id in FORWARD_INSTALL_FOR` with an inline literal `provider_id == "github"` (see `pipeline_advancer.py` change). This is a real maintainability/architecture regression: adding another provider with the same direct-install forwarding behavior now requires editing shared generic code again, and the provider key becomes a duplicated magic string with no central constant or hook. It’s not a functional defect, but it is a concrete, diff-grounded design concern introduced by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The installer-identity check is only enforced on the re-install branch; the first-time-install branch (Integration.DoesNotExist -> pipeline.next_step()) skips the github_authenticated_user vs integration.metadata['sender']['login'] comparison entirely, so the stated security objective of the review iteration is not preserved on the primary path it was added for. An attacker who causes a victim to install the GitHub App (victim is the sender per the webhook) and then completes the Sentry-side flow under their own OAuth identity gets a first-time integration created with no sender match — the exact scenario the accepted fix claims to close — while only the pre-existing-integration path is protected.

adjudication.rationale: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, the GitHub-user vs installer check (`pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`) is only performed in the branch where an `Integration` already exists (and no `OrganizationIntegration` exists). If `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `Integration.DoesNotExist`, the code immediately does `return pipeline.next_step()` with no authenticity/identity verification beyond the earlier OAuth `state` check. This creates an unprotected path for first-time installs where the `Integration` record is not yet present at this step (e.g., webhook not processed yet), so the newly added security objective is not consistently enforced on that path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new hard requirement that the Sentry-side OAuth user equal the original GitHub 'sender' login silently changes the accepted install contract: previously any authenticated org member completing the flow with a valid installation_id could finish setup; review iterations introduced this constraint without a separately accepted change of objective. Legitimate operators get locked out: e.g. an admin who uninstalls/reinstalls after the original 'sender' has left the org or changed their GitHub login can never complete installation — GitHubInstallation returns the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error page with no remediation path, and there is no option/flag to disable the new behavior without a code deploy.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce a new hard gate in `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`: after resolving an existing active `Integration` for the `installation_id`, it now requires `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") == integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` and otherwise returns the generic `error(..., "Invalid installation request.")` (see added block near the end of `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`). This is a concrete behavior/contract change from previously only needing a valid `installation_id` to continue the pipeline, and the error path provides no remediation or override in code. However, the change appears intentional as a security/authenticity verification (new `OAuthLoginView`, new error constant, and an added test `test_github_user_mismatch` asserting the failure), so it’s not clearly a “defect” in correctness so much as a product/UX/backwards-compatibility concern introduced by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Review iterations collapsed three distinct user-facing error messages (invalid request, pending deletion, installed on another org) through one generic default while also replacing the distinct 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' message with the new generic ERR_INTEGRATION_INVALID_INSTALLATION_REQUEST — a user-facing copy change smuggled in by the refactor rather than explicitly accepted. Users hitting the not-found case now see 'Invalid installation request / restart the installation process' instead of the previous accurate message, and support docs/ticket triage keyed to the old strings no longer match; the support-staff-visible contract drifted silently.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce a user-facing copy/behavior change for the “installation not found” path: in `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, if `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` fails, it now returns `error(...)` which defaults to `"Invalid installation request."` / `ERR_INTEGRATION_INVALID_INSTALLATION_REQUEST`, and `test_installation_not_found` was updated accordingly (replacing the prior assertion for “The GitHub installation could not be found.”). However, the claim that three distinct messages were “collapsed” is not accurate: the pending-deletion and installed-on-another-org branches still pass explicit `error_short`/`error_long` values into `error()` preserving distinct messages.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The OAuth authorize redirect is assembled by raw string interpolation (client_id, state, redirect_uri unencoded) instead of urlencode, diverging from how every other OAuth client in the codebase builds this URL. If any of these values ever contain reserved query characters (e.g. a client_id or redirect base with '&' or '='), the authorize URL is silently corrupted and the flow breaks at GitHub with no parseable error; the next person extending this URL inherits a hand-built query string.

adjudication.rationale: In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, the GitHub authorize URL is built via an f-string query (`...?client_id={github_client_id}&state={state}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}`) rather than using `urlencode`/proper quoting. While the current values shown in the diff are likely simple (hex `state`, configured `client_id`, `redirect_uri` from `absolute_uri(reverse(...))` with no querystring), this is a real diff-grounded robustness/maintainability concern: any future addition of params or a redirect URI containing reserved query characters would break the URL parsing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The token-exchange block re-implements OAuth2CallbackView.exchange_token/get_token_params by hand (comment even says 'similar to'), creating a parallel hand-maintained copy of standard OAuth exchange logic including its own swallow-all exception handler that discards the GitHub error response. Any failure mode the shared implementation already handles (error=access_denied callback, non-form-encoded token responses, non-200 exchange responses) gets flattened into the generic 'Invalid installation request.' page with the root cause discarded (the except clause drops req status/body), making the new flow undebuggable for the next change; extracting/reusing the existing view logic would delete this entire duplicate branch set.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `OAuthLoginView.dispatch` which manually performs the OAuth token exchange (`safe_urlopen` to `get_oauth_access_token_url()`, then `safe_urlread` + `parse_qsl`) and explicitly comments it is “similar to OAuth2CallbackView.get_token_params/exchange_token”. It also has a broad `except Exception: payload = {}` and does not check HTTP status or preserve the response body/status for debugging, and it ignores callback `error` parameters (it only looks at `state` and then uses `code`). This is a concrete, diff-grounded maintainability/observability concern (duplicate logic + swallowed diagnostics), but the resulting behavior is still a controlled failure via the generic `error(...)` page rather than a clearly broken or insecure behavior shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new authenticated-sender check is only applied on the branch where the Integration already exists; in the Integration.DoesNotExist branch the pipeline proceeds to the next step with an attacker-supplied installation_id and no verification that the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user owns that installation. A user who completes the GitHub OAuth step as themselves can supply any installation_id that has no existing Sentry Integration row and link that installation (and its repository access) to their own organization, without being the person who installed the GitHub app. The diff adds the sender-vs-authenticated-user check precisely to prevent this, but only guards the already-linked path, leaving the first-install path — the more impactful case — open to the same cross-account claim.

adjudication.rationale: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, the new verification (comparing `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")` to `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`) only runs after confirming an active `Integration` exists (`integration = Integration.objects.get(...);` then mismatch check). If `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `Integration.DoesNotExist` earlier (the first-install path), the code immediately does `return pipeline.next_step()` with whatever `installation_id` came from `request.GET`/pipeline state, and no further check ties that installation_id to the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user established in `OAuthLoginView`. This matches the finding that the authenticated-sender protection is not applied on the `Integration.DoesNotExist` branch, leaving the first-install path unverified in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] raises KeyError for any existing integration whose metadata lacks a 'sender' key, crashing the install flow with a 500 instead of the intended error page. Integrations created before this change (or by code paths that do not store a 'sender' in metadata) hit an unhandled KeyError in GitHubInstallation.dispatch; the user sees a server error rather than the success/failure dialog, and the postMessage contract with the opener window is never satisfied, leaving the installer popup hung.

adjudication.rationale: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, after fetching an existing active `Integration`, the code does `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` with no guard (`try/except` or `.get`). If an existing Integration record has metadata without `sender` (or without `login` under `sender`), this will raise `KeyError` and result in a 500 rather than returning the intended `error(...)` page. The diff shows this new access introduced in the final authenticated-user check block.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] installation_id is bound to pipeline state in two independent places (OAuthLoginView from request.GET, GitHubInstallation from GET-or-state), creating parallel write paths for the same pipeline key with different validation timing. The next maintainer adding validation or normalization to one bind site (e.g. scoping or type-checking the installation_id) will not know the other path bypasses it; the GitHubInstallation view already silently prefers request.GET over the previously-bound state, so a request-supplied installation_id can overwrite the OAuth-step-bound value mid-pipeline.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows two separate bind sites for the same pipeline key: OAuthLoginView.dispatch binds `installation_id` from `request.GET` when present, and GitHubInstallation.dispatch later derives `installation_id = request.GET.get('installation_id', pipeline.fetch_state('installation_id'))` and then `pipeline.bind_state('installation_id', installation_id)`. Because GitHubInstallation prefers the request parameter over the already-bound state, a subsequent request can overwrite the earlier value mid-pipeline. This is a real, diff-grounded maintainability/consistency concern about parallel write paths and differing validation timing, but it is not a directly provable functional defect from the diff alone (no explicit conflicting validation/normalization exists yet).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] test_installation_not_found overwrites the first response with a second client.get and replaces the specific assertion ("The GitHub installation could not be found.") with a generic one ("Invalid installation request."), so the test no longer verifies the not-found behavior it is named for. If the not-found handling regresses (e.g. the new code's DoesNotExist branch inside the try in GitHubInstallation.dispatch returns next_step instead of error), this test still passes as long as any error page is rendered; the specific user-facing 'installation could not be found' message is now completely unasserted, and the first GET's response is silently discarded.

adjudication.rationale: In `test_installation_not_found`, the diff shows two consecutive `self.client.get(...)` calls where the first response (GET with `installation_id`) is immediately overwritten by a second GET (with `code`/`state`), and the assertion was changed from checking `"The GitHub installation could not be found."` to checking `"Invalid installation request."`. As a result, the test no longer asserts any not-found-specific behavior and instead asserts a generic invalid-installation message from the OAuth/state validation path, which makes the test name/intent mismatched and reduces coverage of the not-found scenario.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] test_github_user_mismatch asserts only the generic default error text 'Invalid installation request.', which is the response produced by every failure branch in OAuthLoginView and GitHubInstallation.dispatch (state mismatch, missing access_token, missing login, inactive integration, sender mismatch), so it cannot distinguish the sender-mismatch branch it claims to test from any other failure. Deleting or breaking the new `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` check does not necessarily fail this test: if the mismatch path were silently bypassed (e.g. metadata missing 'sender' raising, or the check inverted in a way that still errors elsewhere), the test passes as long as some failure page renders. The security-critical sender-verification branch has no assertion that specifically confirms the mismatch was the rejection reason.

adjudication.rationale: In `test_github_user_mismatch`, the only content assertion about the failure reason is `b"Invalid installation request."` (plus template used / generic postMessage). The helper `error()` defaults `error_short` to "Invalid installation request." and is returned from multiple distinct failure branches in `OAuthLoginView.dispatch` (missing/invalid state, missing access_token, missing login) and `GitHubInstallation.dispatch` (inactive integration, sender mismatch, etc.). So while the test likely exercises the sender-mismatch path given its setup, it does not assert anything unique to that branch (e.g., a distinct error code/message or that the mismatch comparison was reached), making the test less precise/robust for the security-critical check.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The state value '9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3' is hardcoded and reused verbatim across four different tests and two different organizations, coupling the tests to the exact hash output of pipeline.signature. Any change to how Pipeline.signature is derived (salt, session key, provider key) breaks five assertions simultaneously and forces a blind find-and-replace of a magic constant; a copy-paste error during such a change would make tests assert against a wrong-but-consistent state value and pass while the real state-check logic diverges from what is exercised.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows multiple tests hardcoding the OAuth `state` as `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` and asserting it verbatim (e.g. `assert redirect.query == "client_id=...&state=9cae..."` in `assert_setup_flow`, and repeated `urlencode({"code": ..., "state": "9cae..."})` across `test_github_installed_on_another_org`, `test_github_user_mismatch`, and the pending-deletion tests). This couples the tests to the exact value of `pipeline.signature` and will cause widespread breakage if the signature derivation changes; it's a real test-maintainability issue introduced/expanded by the new OAuth step, but not a product bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] `auth_header = responses.calls[2].request.headers["Authorization"]` is index-coupled to the new OAuth exchange calls registered in _stub_github, asserting on a positional mock-call index rather than on behavior. Adding or reordering any mocked HTTP call in _stub_github (e.g. an extra /user call) silently shifts the index and makes this assertion validate a different request's header — the test keeps passing while verifying the wrong call, or fails confusingly with no behavioral change.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the test to assert `responses.calls[2].request.headers["Authorization"]` (was `[0]`) after adding new mocked HTTP calls in `_stub_github()` (POST `https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token` and GET `/user`). This makes the assertion depend on the exact ordering/count of all HTTP calls during the flow; adding/reordering a mocked call would shift indices and could cause the test to check the wrong request or fail for non-behavioral reasons. This is a test fragility issue, not a production defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] _stub_github now unconditionally registers the OAuth access_token and /user mocks for every test in the class, including tests that do not intend to exercise the OAuth exchange, and no test exercises the failure branches of the exchange (`except Exception: payload = {}` and 'access_token' not in payload). The swallowed-exception path and the missing-access_token path in OAuthLoginView (integration.py lines ~434-437) have zero coverage: a regression that makes safe_urlread failure crash with a 500 instead of rendering the error page would pass CI, because the only mocks registered always return a valid token body.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new error branches in `OAuthLoginView.dispatch` around parsing the token response (`except Exception: payload = {}`) and handling a missing `access_token` (`if "access_token" not in payload: return error(...)`). In tests, `_stub_github` was extended to always mock a successful OAuth token exchange (`body="access_token=..."`) and `/user` (`json={"login": "octocat"}`), and the updated tests exercise only the success path (and a state-mismatch path), not the parse-failure or missing-token branches. This is a specific, diff-grounded test coverage gap for newly added logic, not a functional defect in the implementation shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] In test_github_installed_on_another_org and test_github_prevent_install_until_pending_deletion_is_complete, the initial `resp = self.client.get(self.init_path)` result is immediately overwritten by the follow-up setup_path GET, so no assertion ever inspects the first response. The init step's contract (e.g. that it redirects into the pipeline rather than erroring, and that it does not itself render the failure page) is unverified; if init started rendering the failure page directly the tests would still pass, masking a broken redirect flow behind the overwritten variable.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows both tests overwrite the init response before any assertion: e.g. in `test_github_installed_on_another_org`, `resp = self.client.get(self.init_path_2)` is immediately replaced by `resp = self.client.get(self.setup_path_2)` and assertions (`assertTemplateUsed`, content checks) only inspect the latter. Same pattern in `test_github_prevent_install_until_pending_deletion_is_complete` where the init GET is overwritten by the OAuth callback GET. This means the init step’s behavior (e.g., redirecting into the pipeline vs rendering an error) is not verified by these tests, potentially masking regressions in the init redirect flow.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The state-mismatch rejection branch (`request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`) in OAuthLoginView is reached by no test in the diff; every setup-path test supplies the exact matching signature. A regression that weakens the state comparison (e.g. comparing only a prefix, or accepting any state) would not be caught by any test in this diff, despite this being the CSRF-defensive check the whole OAuth round-trip depends on. Checked test files: tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py — no test sends a mismatched or missing state value to the setup endpoint.

adjudication.rationale: The diff *does* add a test that appears to exercise the OAuth `state` mismatch rejection. In `test_installation_not_found`, after initiating the flow, it calls the setup endpoint with `code=...` and `state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05` and asserts the response contains `Invalid installation request.`. Given `OAuthLoginView.dispatch` rejects when `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` and other tests assert the expected signature/state is `9cae5e...`, this test is specifically sending a mismatched `state` and should hit that branch.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] get_user_info() in OAuthLoginView.dispatch is called outside the try/except that guards the token exchange, so any network/JSON failure fetching /user raises an unhandled exception and the user gets a raw 500 instead of the github-integration-failed error page the rest of the view guarantees. A transient GitHub API outage or malformed /user response during the install pipeline produces an unhandled exception (500 page) mid-pipeline; the pipeline state is left bound (github_authenticated_user never set) and the user sees a server error rather than the 'restart the installation' message every other failure path renders.

adjudication.rationale: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, the call `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is not wrapped in any error handling, even though it is an external call (fetching GitHub /user). If `get_user_info` raises (network error, bad response/JSON), the view will propagate an exception and return a 500 instead of rendering the `github-integration-failed.html` error page used in the other failure branches (`return error(...)`). This unhandled-exception path is visible from the diff (no try/except around `get_user_info`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] integration.metadata['sender']['login'] raises KeyError for an ACTIVE Integration whose metadata lacks a 'sender' key, turning the install request into a 500 instead of the 4xx-style error page the contract of every other rejection path in this view provides. A pre-existing integration row created by an older flow (or by the webhook path before sender was recorded) that has no OrganizationIntegration yet crashes the pipeline with KeyError/500; the user cannot complete or even cleanly fail the install for that installation_id.

adjudication.rationale: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, after fetching an ACTIVE `Integration` (`Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)`), the code unconditionally accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` when validating the authenticated GitHub user. If `metadata` lacks `sender` (or `login`), this will raise `KeyError` and produce a 500 since it is not caught, unlike other rejection paths that return the rendered error page via `error(...)`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The sender-login equality check hard-requires pipeline state 'github_authenticated_user', so any pipeline session created before this deploy (or any entry path that skips OAuthLoginView) fails with None != login and the generic 'Invalid installation request' error during a rolling deploy. Users mid-installation when this code ships have no 'github_authenticated_user' in their session pipeline state; their previously-valid install now dead-ends on the generic error page with no way to distinguish skew from an actual attack, and no feature flag to revert without a code deploy.

adjudication.rationale: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, the new authenticity check unconditionally compares `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")` against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` and errors on mismatch. If the pipeline state lacks `github_authenticated_user` (e.g., an in-progress pipeline created before this change, or any execution that reaches `GitHubInstallation` without having run `OAuthLoginView`), `fetch_state(...)` will be `None`, making the check fail and forcing the generic `Invalid installation request` error. The diff adds no backward-compatible fallback/guard for missing state.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Every failure path in OAuthLoginView (bad state, failed token exchange, missing access_token, missing login) collapses into the identical generic error page with no logging, metric, or distinction, so production failures of the new OAuth exchange are silent and indistinguishable from each other. Operators debugging install failures get zero signal — a GitHub-side token-exchange outage, a state mismatch caused by cache eviction of the pipeline, and an actual forged-state attempt all look identical with no log line or metric, making the 'restart the installation process' advice unverifiable and the failure rate unmeasurable.

adjudication.rationale: In the new `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, multiple distinct failure conditions (`state` mismatch, token exchange/read/parse failure, missing `access_token`, missing `login`) all return `error(request, self.active_organization)` which renders the same `github-integration-failed.html` with the same default message (`ERR_INTEGRATION_INVALID_INSTALLATION_REQUEST`) and there is no logging or `metrics` call anywhere in these branches. This is diff-grounded and creates an observability/debuggability gap for the newly added OAuth exchange, but it’s not a correctness/security defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The authorize redirect URL is built by f-string interpolation without urlencode, so state and redirect_uri (which contains '://', '/', and ':') are injected raw into the query string. The request works only because GitHub's parser tolerates unencoded reserved characters in redirect_uri; any change to the route (e.g. a query param on the setup URL) or stricter GitHub-side parsing silently breaks the OAuth leg, and the value cannot be safely extended without rework.

adjudication.rationale: In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, the GitHub authorize URL is constructed via f-string: `...authorize_url()?client_id=...&state=...&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}` without using `urlencode`/`urllib.parse.urlencode`. The diff shows `redirect_uri` is an absolute URL containing reserved characters (`://`, `/`) and tests explicitly assert the unencoded query string. While this likely works with GitHub today and doesn’t demonstrably break in this diff, it is a diff-grounded robustness/maintainability issue: adding any query params to `redirect_uri` (introducing `?`/`&`) would break the query structure without rework.
